---
title: "Angular SDK"
description: "@seamless-auth/angular adds Seamless Auth to an Angular 20, 21, or 22 application: a signal-based service, functional route guards, an HttpClient interceptor, and optional sign-in screens."
sidebar:
  order: 4.7
---

`@seamless-auth/angular` is the official Angular integration for Seamless Auth. It gives a
standalone Angular application the same session state, auth actions, and optional sign-in screens
the [React SDK](/build/react-sdk) gives a React app, in Angular's own idioms: an injectable service
with signals and observables, a `provideSeamlessAuth()` provider, and functional route guards.

It is a thin binding over `@seamless-auth/client`, the framework-free core the React and React
Native SDKs also build on, so sign-in behaves the same in every binding. The Angular screens keep
the React screens' accessible names, and `seamless verify` runs the same browser specs against both.

---

## How It Fits

```txt
Angular app (browser)
  -> your backend's /auth adapter routes, with signed httpOnly cookies
  -> Seamless Auth API
```

The browser model is the same as React's: the [server adapter](/build/server-sdks) keeps the auth
API's tokens and the browser holds only `httpOnly` cookies on your domain. The Angular SDK has no
bearer mode at all. Its configuration has no transport option, so no token can reach page scripts,
and nothing it writes to browser storage is a credential. See
[Cookie, Session, And Token Reference](/reference/cookies-sessions-tokens).

---

## Requirements

- Angular 20, 21, or 22 (`@angular/core`, `@angular/common`, `@angular/router`) and `rxjs` 7
- A standalone application. Zoneless and zone-based change detection both work, because state is
  held in signals
- A backend mounting the Seamless Auth adapter routes at `/auth`, for example `@seamless-auth/express`

---

## Installation

```bash
npm install @seamless-auth/angular
```

`@seamless-auth/client` comes with it.

---

## Configure The Application

```ts
// app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core'
import { provideHttpClient, withInterceptors } from '@angular/common/http'
import { provideRouter } from '@angular/router'
import { provideSeamlessAuth, seamlessAuthInterceptor } from '@seamless-auth/angular'

import { routes } from './app.routes'

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideRouter(routes),
    provideSeamlessAuth({ apiHost: 'https://app.example.com' }),
    // Optional: sends the session cookies with HttpClient calls to apiHost, and nowhere else.
    provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([seamlessAuthInterceptor])),
  ],
}
```

`apiHost` is the origin your backend serves `/auth` on. The session is read as soon as the
application starts in the browser.

`provideSeamlessAuth` also takes a factory, which runs in an injection context. Use it to read
configuration at runtime, for example from a `config.js` your container writes at startup:

```ts
provideSeamlessAuth(() => ({ apiHost: window.__APP_CONFIG__.apiUrl }))
```

| Option                     | Default          | Purpose                                                             |
| -------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `apiHost`                  | required         | Origin of the server adapter                                        |
| `basePath`                 | `/auth`          | Where the adapter is mounted on `apiHost`                           |
| `magicLinkRedirectUri`     | the deployment's | Where an emailed magic link lands                                   |
| `autoDetectPreviousSignIn` | `true`           | Open the login screen on Sign In for a browser that signed in before |
| `initialSession`           | none             | A session your server already resolved, for server rendering        |
| `ports`                    | browser          | `passkeys` and `oauthRedirect` ports                                |
| `fetch`                    | global `fetch`   | The fetch auth requests go through                                  |
| `signedInPath`             | `/`              | Where the bundled screens go after sign-in                          |
| `loginPath`                | `/login`         | Where `requireAuth` sends someone who is signed out                 |

---

## Protect Routes And Mount The Screens

```ts
// app.routes.ts
import { Routes } from '@angular/router'
import { authGuard, requireAuth } from '@seamless-auth/angular'

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: HomePage, canActivate: [authGuard] },
  { path: 'admin', component: AdminPage, canActivate: [requireAuth({ roles: 'org:admin' })] },
  {
    path: '',
    loadChildren: () => import('@seamless-auth/angular/routes').then((m) => m.seamlessAuthRoutes),
  },
]
```

| Guard                                   | Admits                                     | Otherwise                                                                                          |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `authGuard` / `requireAuth(options?)`   | A signed-in user, with `roles` when given  | `redirectTo` (default `loginPath`). A missing role goes to `forbiddenRedirectTo`, or is refused     |
| `guestGuard` / `requireGuest(options?)` | Someone signed out                         | `redirectTo` (default `signedInPath`)                                                              |

The guards work as `canActivate`, `canActivateChild`, and `canMatch`. They wait for the session to
be read before deciding, so reloading a protected page does not bounce a signed-in user to the login
screen. During a server render without `initialSession`, `requireAuth` treats the request as signed
out and redirects to `loginPath` (since 0.2.0), so a protected page's data never renders into a
response for someone the server could not identify. The browser runs the guards again when the
application boots there.

`roles` uses the same matching as the auth API, scoped roles such as `org:admin` included. A guard
decides what to render; it is not access control. Your backend still checks every request with
`requireAuth`. See [Secure Routes](/build/secure-routes).

Do not put `guestGuard` on `register-passkey`, `oauth/callback`, or `verify-magiclink`. A user can
already have a session by the time those render, and the guard would send them on before they
finish.

---

## The `SeamlessAuth` Service

```ts
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core'
import { Router } from '@angular/router'
import { SeamlessAuth } from '@seamless-auth/angular'

@Component({
  selector: 'app-account-menu',
  template: `
    @if (auth.user(); as user) {
      <span>{{ user.email }}</span>
      <button type="button" (click)="signOut()">Logout</button>
    }
  `,
})
export class AccountMenu {
  protected readonly auth = inject(SeamlessAuth)
  private readonly router = inject(Router)

  async signOut() {
    await this.auth.logout()
    await this.router.navigateByUrl('/login')
  }
}
```

- **Signals:** `state`, `user`, `isAuthenticated`, `loading`, `credentials`, `organizations`,
  `activeOrganization`, `stepUpStatus`, `hasSignedInBefore`, plus `loginMethods`,
  `loginMethodsLoading`, `passkeySupported`, and `passkeySupportLoading`.
- **Observables:** `state$`, `user$`, `isAuthenticated$`. Each emits the current value on subscribe.
- **Actions:** `login`, `handlePasskeyLogin`, `registerPasskey`, `refreshSession`, `logout`,
  `logoutAllSessions`, `deleteUser`, `updateCredential`, `deleteCredential`, `switchOrganization`,
  `listOAuthProviders`, `startOAuthLogin`, `finishOAuthLogin`, `refreshStepUpStatus`,
  `verifyStepUpWithPasskey`, `verifyStepUpWithPasskeyPrf`, and `verifyStepUpWithTotp`.
- **Also:** `hasRole`, `hasScopedRole`, `markSignedIn`, `whenSettled()`, `loadLoginMethods()` and
  `checkPasskeySupport()` (each read once and cached), `authorizedFetch`, `client` (the headless
  client for OTP, magic link, organization, and TOTP calls), and `ports`.

Every request action resolves to a `SeamlessAuthResult<T>`, `{ data, error }`, and does not throw
for an HTTP or network failure, the same convention as the React SDK.

---

## Built-In Screens

`@seamless-auth/angular/routes` exports `seamlessAuthRoutes` and the standalone components behind
them. The screens move between each other relative to their parent route, so they work at the root
or under a path such as `{ path: 'account', children: seamlessAuthRoutes }`. The array has no
wildcard route, so mounting it at the root does not swallow your own unknown paths.

| Path               | Component           | Purpose                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `login`            | `SaLogin`           | Sign in with an email or phone number, or create an account   |
| `passkey-login`    | `SaPasskeyLogin`    | Sign in with a passkey alone                                  |
| `verify-email-otp` | `SaVerifyOtp`       | Check an email code                                           |
| `verify-phone-otp` | `SaVerifyOtp`       | Check a text message code                                     |
| `magic-link-sent`  | `SaMagicLinkSent`   | Wait for an emailed link to be used                           |
| `verify-magiclink` | `SaVerifyMagicLink` | Where the emailed link lands. The auth API builds this URL    |
| `oauth/callback`   | `SaOAuthCallback`   | The OAuth redirect URI to register with your providers        |
| `register-passkey` | `SaRegisterPasskey` | Offer passkey enrolment after sign-up                         |

The building blocks are exported too: `SaOtpInput` (bind it with `[(value)]`), `SaFallbackOptions`,
`SaOAuthProviderButtons`, `SaAuthLayout`, `authRoutePaths`, and `injectAuthNavigation`.

The magic link and OAuth callback screens remove the token or code from the address bar once they
have read it, so a single-use secret does not stay in history or travel in a `Referer`.

### Styling

The screens render inside `.sa-auth` with plain `.sa-*` classes and one unencapsulated stylesheet,
so your global styles can override any rule. Colors come from the same `--seamless-*` custom
properties the React screens read, so one theme covers both:

```css
:root {
  --seamless-accent: #1f3a34;
  --seamless-accent-hover: #16302b;
  --seamless-surface: #f7f5f0;
  --seamless-surface-raised: #ffffff;
  --seamless-text: #1a1a1a;
  --seamless-text-muted: #4b5563;
}
```

The full token list is in the
[`@seamless-auth/react` README](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-react/tree/main/packages/react#theming-the-built-in-ui). The stylesheet also
ships as `@seamless-auth/angular/seamless-auth.css` if you want a copy to start from.

---

## Custom Screens

Every bundled screen is a thin view over a flow in `@seamless-auth/client`: `beginSignIn`,
`registerWithEmail`, `requestOtp` and `verifyOtp`, `watchMagicLink` and `finishMagicLinkSignIn`,
`startOAuthSignIn` and `completeOAuthCallback`, `enrollPasskey`, plus helpers such as
`loadLoginMethods`, `fallbackSignInOptions`, and `safeReturnPath`. A custom screen calls the same
flows, passing the service as its actions:

```ts
import { beginSignIn } from '@seamless-auth/client'

const step = await beginSignIn(auth, {
  identifier: email,
  passkeySupported: await auth.checkPasskeySupport(),
  configuredMethods: await auth.loadLoginMethods(),
})

if (step.kind === 'signed_in') await router.navigateByUrl('/')
if (step.kind === 'choose_method') showOtherMethods(step.loginMethods)
if (step.kind === 'error') showError(step.message)
```

[How To Build Your Own Auth UI](/build/custom-auth-ui) walks through the flows in order. Its
examples use React hooks, but the client calls are the same.

---

## Server Rendering

On the server the service does not read the session or browser storage, and the screens start no
requests: a server render has none of the browser's cookies, and a magic link or OAuth code is
single use. `loading` stays true unless you pass `initialSession`. To render a known session on the
first paint, resolve it on your server through your adapter and hand it over as `initialSession`;
the browser then revalidates it in the background. Do not forward the browser's cookies to the
adapter's `/auth/users/me` from a server.
